# Research notes on Genesis 46 for a verse-by-verse commentary

**What I could and couldn't find.** I ran out of searches before I could check several of the sites you listed, so the following are missing:
- Spurgeon (except one quote that Guzik uses), Ligonier, Desiring God, GTY, Seedbed, the Lutheran sites and Pentecostal sources other than Guzik
- NET Bible notes and Bible Odyssey
- The Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). StudyLight lists a Haydock Catholic commentary on Genesis 46, but I didn't get to open it.
- Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter

Gill shows up only in short excerpts. Also, the sources I read didn't line up neatly by denomination. The real disagreements are between individual commentators, mostly over the number 70 versus 75 in vv. 26–27 and how to read v. 4. Points marked "(Pulpit)", "(Calvin)" or "(Utley)" come from full pages I read; their URLs are given at the end of each point.

---

**v. 1**
- Beersheba was the last stop in Canaan on the road to Egypt. Jacob left nothing behind, and came to the southernmost outpost of Canaan on the way to Egypt. Israel stopped there to honor God with sacrifices. Guzik quotes Spurgeon saying it was a turning point in Jacob's life that called for special waiting on the Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Ellicott: Jacob's first joy gave way to second thoughts, so he decided to consult God first. No place could be more suitable than Beersheba, as both Abraham and Isaac had built altars there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-46.html
- Matthew Henry: Isaac had been told not to go to Egypt (Gen 26:2), and Jacob may have remembered this. In effect he was praying that if God forbade him, he would stay. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_046.cfm
- Benson (Methodist): these were extra sacrifices. They thanked God that Joseph was alive and asked for guidance about leaving Canaan for the idolatrous country of Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/genesis-46.html
- Clarke (Methodist) goes further: it is very likely that he offered his sacrifice merely to obtain this information. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-46.html
- Calvin (Reformed): Jacob was about to lose sight of a land that pictured and pledged the heavenly country. The sacrifice renewed his memory of the covenant so his faith would not fail. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-46.html
- Utley (bible.org): usually sacrifice comes after God appears, but here Jacob sacrifices first because he wants confirmation. Calling God "the God of his father Isaac" stresses the covenant God; it is not a sign that Jacob lacked personal faith. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46

**v. 2**
- Guzik: More than 40 years before, when Jacob was about to leave the Promised Land, God spoke to him in a dream (Genesis 28:12-17). Now, when he was about to leave the land again, God again brought assurance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Calvin: the vision shows God accepted the sacrifice. A vision without words would have helped little; the word is "the soul of the vision." From this he attacks Catholic sacraments as signs without the word. That is a clear Protestant–Catholic difference, but it is Calvin's own aside, not a reading of the verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-46.html
- Pulpit: using the name "Jacob" may remind him of what he once was, and saying it twice makes him pay closer attention. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html
- Utley: the double name is a sign of affection. "Here I am" is the usual reply to God. This is the last night vision given to a patriarch; God never speaks to Joseph this way. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46

**v. 3**
- Why was Jacob afraid? Guzik points to Abraham's bad experience in Egypt (Gen 12) and the warning of 400 years of slavery (Gen 15:13). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Benson lists four fears: his age (130), the danger of Egyptian idolatry for his sons, the prophecy of bondage, and not wanting to be buried in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/genesis-46.html
- Guzik on "a great nation there": Because of the exclusive, segregated nature of Egyptian life, Israel's descendants could grow as a large, distinct nation there. Egypt became like a mother's womb to Israel as a nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Constable: this is one of four "do not be afraid" consolations that God gave in Genesis (Genesis 46:3; cf. Genesis 15:1; Genesis 21:17; Genesis 26:24). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/46-4.html
- Utley: in Hebrew the title is literally "the El, the Elohim of your father." The promise of becoming a nation "there" in Egypt is new. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46

**v. 4** (the most discussed verse)
- *"I will go down with you."* Henry: Those that go whither God sends them shall certainly have God with them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_046.cfm
- Pulpit: this does not mean the Hebrews believed in a local god who moved with them. It is a picture of complete divine protection. Utley adds that it shows God is not limited to Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html ; https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46
- *"I will surely bring you back": who comes back?* Commentators differ here.
  - Calvin: the promise is not about Jacob himself but his descendants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-46.html
  - Poole: though not in thy person, yet in thy body, Genesis 47:29,30 50:5,13; and in thy posterity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/46-4.htm
  - JFB: it came true literally when Jacob's body was taken back to Canaan, but fully only when Israel settled in the land. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_046.cfm
  - The Cambridge note on the same Bible Hub page says They foretell the Exodus of the Israelites, not the burial of Jacob. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/46-4.htm
  - Constable takes both: the return 400 years later and Jacob's burial. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/46-4.html
- *"Joseph's hands will close your eyes."* All agree this was an ancient custom done by the closest relative.
  - Ellicott: The promise conveyed the assurance that Jacob would die peacefully, surrounded by his friends. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-46.html
  - Henry (Puritan/Presbyterian) thinks Jacob had wished for this, and God sometimes gratifies the innocent wishes of his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/46-4.html
  - Calvin is more cautious: the wish involved some infirmity of the flesh, but God granted it to ease the grief of a new exile. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/46-4.html
  - Trapp: Joseph closes eyes that will one day "see God" in the flesh, a link to resurrection hope. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/genesis-46.html
  - Pulpit sums up a fourfold promise: enlargement, protection, restoration, consolation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html

**v. 5**
- Calvin and Pulpit: "rose up" suggests Jacob got new strength from the vision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-46.html
- Guzik: the wagons mattered because seeing them had revived Jacob's spirit (45:27). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Bible Hub study notes: the family's move under Egyptian escort foreshadows Israel's later departure under divine escort at the Exodus. https://biblehub.com/genesis/46.htm

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: taking everyone shows great faith. No one was left behind to continue a presence in Canaan. Jacob was both all in, and he *knew* they would be back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Pulpit: Jacob took his own goods rather than lean too heavily on Pharaoh's generosity. A tomb painting at Beni Hasan of Semitic travellers entering Egypt may illustrate the scene, though Pulpit doesn't claim it shows Jacob. Calvin's editor and Ellicott mention the same painting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html
- Clarke dates this to Jacob's 130th year, 215 years after the promise to Abraham. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-46.html
- Utley: scholars ask whether "daughters" means more daughters than Dinah, or daughters-in-law. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: "who went to Egypt" must be read loosely. The list includes Joseph, his sons and probably some grandsons born later in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html
- Utley: because dead sons (Er and Onan) are named, he thinks the list came from a different setting. In his view that doesn't make it inaccurate, just not written for this exact moment. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46

**vv. 9–11**
- Pulpit gives name meanings and notes different spellings in Numbers 26 and 1 Chronicles. Utley gives a table of these differences and explains them as oral tradition or people having two names. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html ; https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46
- v. 10, Shaul "son of a Canaanite woman":
  - Calvin: Moses means to mark this line with dishonour, because the fathers were not to marry Canaanites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-46.html
  - Pulpit: the other sons' wives, except Judah's, were probably from Mesopotamia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html
  - Utley notes Rashi's Jewish tradition that Shaul was Dinah's child by Shechem. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-46

**v. 12**
- Guzik: Judah's line matters most because it leads to the Messiah: Abraham to Isaac to Jacob to Judah to Perez to Hezron (Luke 3:33-34). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Hezron and Hamul's timing is a puzzle. Clarke says Perez was probably too young, so they must have been born during Jacob's 17 years in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-46.html
- Ellicott: there is no space whatsoever for their births before the move. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-46.html

**v. 13**
- "Job" is probably meant to be Jashub, as in Numbers 26:24 and 1 Chronicles 7:1, and the Greek Septuagint (LXX) reads it that way. (Pulpit; Utley) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html

**v. 15**
- Thirty-two names are listed but the total is 33.
  - Calvin counts Jacob himself as the first of the 33. He rejects the Jewish view that Jochebed, Moses' mother, is included. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-46.html
  - Pulpit also counts Jacob and leaves out Er and Onan. It suggests Dinah stayed unmarried after Shechem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html

**v. 17**
- Calvin guesses that Serah and Dinah are named because they were unmarried. (Calvin)

**v. 20**
- The Greek Septuagint adds five descendants of Manasseh and Ephraim here, probably taken from 1 Chronicles 7. Pulpit cites Rosenmüller's view that this began as a margin note. (Pulpit)

**v. 21**
- In Numbers 26 Naaman and Ard appear as Benjamin's grandsons. A common explanation is that some of Benjamin's sons died early and grandsons named after them took their place. (Pulpit)

**vv. 26–27** (66, 70 or 75? Here the commentators clearly disagree.)
- The usual count: 66 plus Jacob, Joseph and his two sons makes 70 (Guzik, Benson). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Stephen says 75 in Acts 7:14. Most agree he is following the Septuagint, which gives the number at seventy-five, and makes it up by inserting the son and grandson of Manasseh, two sons and a grandson of Ephraim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-14.htm
- How the commentators handle it:
  - **Calvin (Reformed):** an error of the transcribers. He rejects Augustine's view that Stephen counted ahead to people born later. He would accept that Luke adapted himself to readers used to the Greek. His main point is that the small number makes God's later blessing shine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-46.html
  - **Clarke (Methodist), following Hales:** add the nine wives of Jacob's sons to the 66, giving 75, which critically corresponding with the statement in the New Testament. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-46.html
  - **Gill (Baptist):** take out Joseph, his sons, Hezron and Hamul to get 64, then add the eleven wives of Jacob's sons to reach 75. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/acts/7-14.html
  - **Pulpit:** the numbers count different groups, so How are we to understand the lists? has an answer and there is no real contradiction. Ellicott: Stephen, a Greek-speaking Jew, simply used his Greek Bible's number. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-14.htm
  - **Guzik:** The number in the Septuagint is not wrong, just arrived at in a different way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
  - **Bible Hub Q&A:** both are two legitimate textual traditions. https://biblehub.com/q/how_to_reconcile_acts_7_14_and_gen_46_27.htm
- Guzik's application: God's greatest works often have slow, humble beginnings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/

**v. 28**
- Pulpit: Jacob trusted Judah because of the noble character he had shown. "To get directions" means Joseph would guide them to their settlement, not that he would meet them there. The Septuagint reads "land of Rameses" instead of Goshen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-46.html
- Guzik (Spanish edition): it was fitting for Judah, of the Messiah's line, since he showed real repentance. https://es.enduringword.com/comentario-biblico/genesis-46/
- Calvin: Jacob only wanted leave to pitch his tents peacefully, so as not to provoke the locals. (Calvin)

**v. 29**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew word for Joseph "presenting himself" is the one normally used when God or angels appear, which shows the splendour in which he came. Most take Joseph as the one who fell on his father's neck. (Pulpit)
- Calvin: the scene shows the fathers had natural feelings. Feelings need to be kept within bounds, not rooted out. (Calvin)

**v. 30**
- Pulpit: Jacob's last earthly longing was satisfied, and he was ready to die whenever God willed. (Pulpit)
- Trapp, quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, applies it to Christ: what should it be to us, that Christ was dead and is alive. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-46.html

**vv. 31–32**
- Guzik: Joseph became the representative and the advocate for the whole family. They came to safety in Egypt but needed Joseph to represent them. In the same pattern, the believer needs Jesus Christ to represent him or her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
- Henry: once the brothers plotted to get rid of Joseph; now he is contriving to settle them to their advantage; this is rendering good for evil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/46-34.htm

**vv. 33–34**
- Was Joseph being crafty? Calvin raises the question and says no. Pharaoh already knew Goshen was fertile and had offered the best land himself. Joseph was being modest, and the reason he gave was true. Being despised kept the church from being scattered, and God often lets the world reject us so we stay clean of its pollution. (Calvin)
- Henry: Joseph wanted them not to be ashamed of honest work. An honest calling is no disgrace. https://biblehub.com/par/genesis/46-34.htm
- Pulpit: asking a man's occupation fitted Egypt's caste system. Joseph wanted Goshen for three reasons: good pasture, separation from Egyptians, and nearness to Canaan for the eventual return. (Pulpit)
- Why were shepherds hated? The explanations differ:
  - They killed animals the Egyptians worshipped (Ellicott, Benson, Clarke's "best reason").
  - Memories of the Hyksos "shepherd kings" (Barnes, Clarke).
  - Settled farmers despise nomads (Constable, Keil and Delitzsch).
  - Pulpit doubts the Hyksos theory and prefers the farmers-versus-nomads view.
  - Gill rejects the animal-worship explanation. He says only foreign shepherds were meant, since Egypt had its own respected herdsmen.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/46-34.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/46-34.html
- Ellicott and Pulpit: the words "all shepherds are detestable" are probably the narrator's comment, not Joseph's. Egyptian monuments back them up by drawing herdsmen as unshaven and deformed. https://biblehub.com/genesis/46-34.htm
- Guzik: God had a place for His people, but it was a different place and a place despised by some people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-46/
